entries.title: nanoMuse 1.0.9 · Tiller
entries.note: nanoMuse 1.0.9 · Tiller 🐉 nanoMuse 1.0.9 “Tiller” : a fix release the same day as Crew. The desktop starts again when you are signed in, the relay's console loads on a large record, and the runtime takes a budget for a task and recalls from the whole memory store. 1.0.8 went out this morning, and its desktop did not start for anyone who was signed in. The plugin pointed the nanoMuse Cloud provider row at the loopback door it opens for the relay and waited for that settings write while the plugins were still starting; the write waits for the plugins, so the Host never announced its address and the window sat on Starting… for good, with nanoMuse is still starting every ten minutes ( #701 , fixed in #703 ). entries.title: nanoMuse 1.0.8 · Crew
entries.note: nanoMuse 1.0.8 · Crew 🐉 nanoMuse 1.0.8 “Crew” : four days after Logbook, your devices keep each other posted. A scheduled task on the computer that needs a yes asks on your phone; every device reads the step another is on and says when it is waiting for you; the wait before a first token is spoken of, with your place in the queue; a thumb on a reply or the reason for a Stop goes to the account's record as one word, and the operator reads the record question by question. The phone no longer crashes when you stop talking, the iPhone no longer stops your music, the desktop's Library takes documents of your own, and the runtime behaves on Windows. 1.0.7 went out on 2026-10-25. Since then seventy-two pull requests were merged, and this version is the fifth look at the whole project, with one change at its centre: the devices keep each other posted . entries.title: nanoMuse 1.0.7 · Logbook

Since then twenty-seven pull requests were merged, and this version is the fourth look at the whole project, with one change at its centre: the record . entries.title: nanoMuse 1.0.6 · Beacon
entries.note: nanoMuse 1.0.6 · Beacon 🐉 nanoMuse 1.0.6 “Beacon” : nine days after Lookout, a third look at the whole project with the forty-eight pull requests that arrived in between; nanoMuse Cloud serves one multimodal model and leaves pictures and clips to a provider of your own, the relay's sign-in gives nothing away, the runtime finishes what a restart interrupted, the desktop asks before a restart, and the phone reads the Feed posts you liked. 1.0.5 went out on 2026-10-14. Since then forty-eight pull requests were merged, more than in any week before, and this version reads the project through once more with them in: the relay, the Python runtime, the web console, the desktop, the Android and iPhone apps, the docs and the workflows, area by area. entries.title: nanoMuse 1.0.5 · Lookout
entries.note: nanoMuse 1.0.5 · Lookout 🐉 nanoMuse 1.0.5 “Lookout” : the day after Compass, a second look at the whole project together with the day's reports; the daily feed is written out of sight, the Android approval card fits the screen, the desktop's dead buttons work and a quit protects the work in progress, the Windows release can update itself, and the relay's console finds anything. 1.0.4 went out on 2026-10-13. The same day we read nanoMuse through once more, this time with the reports and pull requests that arrived while Compass was being built, and nine passes again went over the relay, the Python runtime, the web console, the desktop, the Android and iPhone apps, the hosted showcase, the documentation and the workflows ( #444 to #455 ). entries.note: nanoMuse 1.0.1 · Ballast 🐉 nanoMuse 1.0.1 “Ballast” : the first day of 1.0 in people's hands, read back; what broke for them is fixed, and what two apps on one phone fought over is settled. 1.0.0 went out on 2026-10-09. entries.title: nanoMuse 1.0.0 · Keel
entries.note: nanoMuse 1.0.0 · Keel 🐉 nanoMuse 1.0.0 “Keel” : the first stable version, one personal agent for every device you own, and nothing in it that we would not run ourselves. Since 2026-09-25 every version has been a preview. Forty of them later the set is complete: a phone app for Android and for the iPhone, a desktop app for the Mac, Windows and Linux, the web console, and the open-source relay, nanoMuse Cloud, that signs people in and lets their devices talk. One account across all of them, so the phone, the desktop and the browser show the same conversation. Hands on the phone and on the computer, which look at the screen and act for you, with an approval between the agent and anything you could not undo.
